questions.q: If the line $y = xtan\theta$~cuts the curve $x^{3} + xy^{2} + 2x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3x + 1 = 0$~at the points $A, B$~and $C$. If $OA, OB$ and $OC$ are in $HP$, then $tan\theta$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,

line& $y = xtan\theta$~cuts the curve~$x^{3} + xy^{2} + 2x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3x + 1 = 0 \ldots \left(i\right)$~at three points~$A, B$~and~$C$.

Let us assume~$A \left({x}_{1}, {{x}_{1}tan\theta\right),~$B \left({x}_{2}, {x}_{2}$tan$\theta\right)~and~$C \left({x}_{3}, {x}_{3}tan\theta\right)$

$⇒ OA = \sqrt{{x1}^{2} + {x1}^{2}\tan^{2}\theta}$

$= {x}_{1}\sqrt{1 + \tan^{2}\theta} = {x}_{1}sec\theta$

Similarly~$OB = {x}_{2}sec\theta$~and~$OC = {x}_{3}sec\theta$

$∵ OA, OB, OC$~in $H . P .$

$⇒OB = \dfrac{2 \cdot \left(OA\right)\left(OC\right)}{OA + OC}$

$⇒ {x}_{2} \cdot sec\theta = \dfrac{2{x}_{1} \cdot {x}_{3}\sec^{2}\theta}{\left({x}_{1} + {x}_{3}\right)sec\theta}$

$⇒ {x}_{1}{x}_{2} + {x}_{2}{x}_{3} = 2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$

$⇒ {x}_{1}{x}_{2} + {x}_{2}{x}_{3} + {x}_{3}{x}_{1} = 3{x}_{1}{x}_{3} \ldots \left(ii\right)$.

Now, substitute~$y = xtan\theta$~in equation~ \left($i\right)$, we get

$x^{3} + x^{3}\tan^{2}$\theta +$2x^{2} + 2x^{2}\tan^{2}$\theta +$3x + 1 = 0$

$⇒ x^{3}\sec^{2}$\theta +$2x^{2}\sec^{2}$\theta +$3x + 1 = 0 \ldots \left(iii\right)$

Now, the roots of the equation~ \left(iii\right)$~will be~${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}, {x}_{3}$.

$⇒ {x}_{1} \cdot {x}_{2} + {x}_{2} \cdot {x}_{3} + {x}_{3} \cdot {x}_{1} = $\dfrac{3}{\sec^{2}\theta} \ldots \left(iv\right)$

$⇒ {x}_{1} \cdot {x}_{2} \cdot {x}_{3} = - $\dfrac{1}{\sec^{2}\theta} \ldots \left(v\right)$~

From equations~ \left(ii\right)$~and~ \left(iv\right)$,~$3{x}_{1}{x}_{3} = \dfrac{3}{\sec^{2}\theta}$

$⇒ {x}_{1}{x}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sec^{2}\theta} \ldots \left(vi\right)$

From equations~ \left($v\right)$~and~ \left(vi\right)$,~${x}_{2} = - 1$

$∵ {x}_{2}$~is one of the roots of the equation~ \left($iii\right)$, so it will satisfy the equation.

$⇒ - \sec^{2}$\theta +$2\sec^{2}$\theta -$3 + 1 = 0$

$⇒ \sec^{2}$\theta =$2$

$⇒ sec$\theta = \pm $\sqrt{2}$

$⇒ tan$\theta = \pm$1$.

questions.q: Let $A \left(-1, 1\right), B  \left($3, 4\right)$~and $C  \left(2, 0\right)$ be given three points. A line $y = mx, m > 0$~, intersects lines $AC$ and $BC$~at point $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Let ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ be the areas of $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta PQC$~respectively, such that ${A}_{1} = 3{A}_{2}$, then the value of $m$ is equal to :$
questions.solution:
$P ≡ \left({x}_{1},m{x}_{1}\right)$

~$Q ≡ \left({x}_{2},m{x}_{2}\right)$

${A}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}3 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ - 1 & 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{13}{2}$

${A}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}{x}_{1}& m{x}_{1} & 1 \\ {x}_{2} & m{x}_{2} & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

${A}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|2\left(m{x}_{1} - m{x}_{2}\right)\right| = m\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right|$

${A}_{1} = 3{A}_{2} ⇒ \dfrac{13}{2} =$=3m\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right|$

$⇒ \left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| = $\dfrac{16}{6m}

$AC: x + 3y = 2$

$BC: y = 4x - 8$

$P: x + 3y = 2 & y = mx ⇒ {x}_{1} = $\dfrac{2}{1 + 3m}

$Q: y = 4x - 8 & y = mx ⇒ {x}_{2} = $\dfrac{8}{4 - m}

\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| = \left|$\dfrac{2}{1 + 3m} - \dfrac{8}{4 - m}\right|

$= \left|$\dfrac{- 26m}{\left(1 + 3m\right)\left(4 - m\right)}\right| = \dfrac{26m}{\left(3m + 1\right)\left|m - 4\right|}

$= $\dfrac{26m}{\left(3m + 1\right) \left($4 - m\right)}

\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| = \dfrac{13}{6m}$

$\dfrac{26m}{\left(3m + 1\right) \left(4 - m\r$right)}=\dfrac{13}{6m}

$⇒ 12m^{2} = - \left(3m + 1\right)\left(m - 4\right)$

$⇒ 12m^{2} = - \left(3m^{2} - 11m - 4\right)$

$⇒ 15m^{2} - 11m - 4 = 0$

$⇒ 15m^{2} - 15m + 4m - 4 = 0$

$⇒ \left(15m + 4\$right)\left($m - 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ m = 1$

$

questions.solution: As per condition given, we write $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{p}_{1}$&=$\frac{|-5 \cos 2 \theta|}{\sqrt{\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta}} \text { and }$p_{2}=$\frac{|-5|}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta+\sec ^{2} \theta}}$\\ \therefore $\mathrm{p}_{1}^{2}=\frac{25 \cos ^{2} 2 \theta}{1} \text { and }$4 $\mathrm{p}_{2}^{2}$&=$\frac{4(25)}{\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta+\sec ^{2} \theta}$\\ \therefore $\mathrm{p}_{1}^{2}+$4 $\mathrm{p}_{2}^{2}$&=25\left(\cos ^{2} \theta-\sin ^{2} \theta\right)^{2}+\frac{100}{\left(\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \theta}\right)+\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} \theta}}$\\ \text{ and } =25(\cos $\theta-\sin \theta)^{2}(\cos \theta+\sin \theta)^{2}+$100 \sin ^{2} $\theta \cos ^{2} \theta$\\ \text{ and } =25(1-\sin 2 $\theta)($1+\sin 2 $\theta)+$25  \left($4 \sin ^{2} $\theta \cos ^{2} \theta\right)$\\ \text{ and } =25\left($1-\sin 2 $\theta+\sin$2 $\theta-\sin ^{2}$2 $\theta\right)+$25(2 \sin $\theta \cos \theta)^{2}$\\ &=25\left($1-\sin ^{2} 2 $\theta\right)+$25(\sin 2 $\theta)^{2}$\\ \text{ and } =25\left(\cos ^{2}$2 $\theta\right)+$25\left(\sin ^{2}$2 $\theta\right)=25 \end{aligned} $

questions.solution: Given equation of pair of lines is $2 x^2+4 x y-p y^2+4 x+q y+1=0$ Comparing with $\mathrm{a} x^2+2 \mathrm{~h} x y+\mathrm{b} y^2+2 \mathrm{~g} x+2 \mathrm{f} y+\mathrm{c}=0$, we get $\mathrm{a}=2, \mathrm{~h}=2, \mathrm{~b}=-\mathrm{p}$ If the given equation represents a pair of straight lines, then $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}^2 \geq \mathrm{ab} \\ & \Rightarrow 4 \geq-2 \mathrm{p} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \geq-\mathrm{p} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{p} \geq-2 \end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Possible values of $\mathrm{p}$ from domain $[-5,5]$ are $-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4,5$. $\therefore \quad$ Number of integral values of $p=8$

questions.q: If the axes are rotated through an angle $45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$ in the positive direction without changing the origin, then the co-ordinates of the point $(\sqrt{2}, 4)$ in the old system are
questions.solution:
If $\theta$ is the angle of rotation, then the co-ordinates in the new system are $x^{\prime}=x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta$, $y^{\prime}=y \cos \theta-x \sin \theta$
Given that $x^{\prime}=\sqrt{2}, y^{\prime}=4$
Thus, $x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta=\sqrt{2}$
y \cos $\theta-$x \sin $\theta=$4 Also, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4} \Rightarrow x \cos \frac{\pi}{4}+y \sin \frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt{2}$
and $y \cos \frac{\pi}{4}-x \sin \frac{\pi}{4}=4\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow$& x+y=2 \\
$\text { and }$& y-x=4 $\sqrt{2}
\end{array}$On adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $2 y=2+4 \sqrt{2}\Rightarrow \quad y=1+2 \sqrt{2}$
On subtracting (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & 2 x & =2-4 $\sqrt{2}$\\
& x & =1-2 $\sqrt{2}
\end{array} \Rightarrow \quad$x=1-2 $\sqrt{2}$Thus, the co-ordinates of $(\sqrt{2}, 4)$ in the old system $(1-2 \sqrt{2}, 1+2 \sqrt{2})$

questions.q: The transformed equation of $3 x^2+3 y^2+2 x y=2$, when the coordinate axes are rotated through an angle of $45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$, is
questions.solution:
Since, the axes are rotated through an angle $45^{\circ}$, then we replace $(x, y)$ by  \left(x \cos 45^{\circ}-y \sin 45^{\circ}, x \sin 45^{\circ}+y \cos 45^{\circ}\right)$ ie, $\quad $\$left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}\right) in the given equation $3 x^2+3 y^2+2 x y=2\begin{array}{rrr}
\therefore \quad$3\$left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2+3\$left(\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \\
& +2\$left(\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=$2 \\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{3}{2}\left($x^2+y^2+2 x y\$right)+\frac{3}{2}\left($x^2+y^2-2 x y\right) \\
& & $+\frac{2}{2}\left($x^2-y^2\right)=2 \\
\Rightarrow & 4 x^2+2 y^2=2 \\
\Rightarrow & 2 x^2+y^2=1
\end{array}
$

questions.q: Let $a \ne 0, b \ne 0, c$ be three real numbers and $L\left(p, q\right) = \dfrac{ap + bq + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}}, ∀ p, q \in R$.~If $L\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right) + L\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right) + L ( 2, 2 ) = 0$, then the line $ax + by + c = 0$ always passes through the fixed point
questions.solution:
Given that $L\left(p, q\right) = \dfrac{ap + bq + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}}$.

$L\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{a\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) + b\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \dfrac{2a + b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}}$

$L\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{a\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + b\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \dfrac{a + 2b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}}$

$L\left(2, 2\right) = \dfrac{a\left(2\right) + b\left(2\right) + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \dfrac{2a + 2b + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \dfrac{6a + 6b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}}$

$L \left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right) ++L\$left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right) ++$L \left(2, 2\right)$

$= \dfrac{2a + b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}} + \dfrac{a + 2b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}} + \dfrac{6a + 6b + 3c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}}$

$= \dfrac{9a + 9b + 9c}{3\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}} =0$

$∴ 9a + 9b + 9c = 0 ⇒ a + b + c = 0 . . . \left(1\right)$

By verifying the options

Substitute $( 1, 1 )$ in the given equation of line,

$a \left(1\right) + b \left($1\right) + c = 0 . . . \left($2\right)$

$

Here, $\mathrm{x}_1=\alpha, \mathrm{y}_1=2 \alpha-1, \mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=-2, \mathrm{c}=4\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{\mathrm{x}-\alpha}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z} \alpha+1}{-2}=\frac{-2(3(\alpha)+(-2)(2 \alpha-1)+4}{3^2+2^2}$\\ & $\frac{\mathrm{x}-\alpha}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z} \alpha+1}{-2}=\frac{-2}{13}(-\alpha+$6) \end{aligned} compare variable terms with constant term $\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{\mathrm{x}-\alpha}{3}=\frac{-12}{13}(-\alpha+$6) \\ & 13 $\mathrm{x}-$13 $\alpha=-$6(-$\alpha+$6) \\ & 13 $\mathrm{x}-$13 $\alpha=$6 $\alpha+$36 \\ & 13 $\mathrm{x}+$36=19 $\alpha \end{aligned}$
Now, $\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{\mathrm{y}-2 \alpha+1}{-2}=\frac{-2}{13}(-\alpha+$6) \\ & 13 $\mathrm{y}-$26 $\alpha+$13=4(-$\alpha+$6) \\ & 13 $\mathrm{y}-$26 $\alpha+$13+4 $\alpha-$24=0 \end{aligned} $13 y-11==22 \alpha$
compare equation (i) and (ii) $\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{13 x+36}{19}=\frac{13 y-11}{22}$\\ & 22(13 x+36)=19(13 y-11) \end{aligned}

questions.q: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is divided by the diagonal $AC$ into two triangles of equal areas. If $A, B, C$ are respectively \left(3, 4\right),  \left(-3, 6\right), \left(-$5, 1\right)$, then the locus of $D is$
questions.solution:
Given points are $A ( 3, 4 ) , B ( - 3, 6 ) , C ( - 5, 1 ) , D ( x, y )$.

Here area of $ABC =$Area of $ACD$.

Area of $ABC = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|∑ {x}_{1}\left({y}_{2} - {y}_{3}\right)\right|$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|3\left(6 - 1\right) + \left(- 3\right)\left(1 - 4\right) + \left(- 5\right)\left(4 - 6\right)\right|$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|3 \left($5\right) + \left(- 3\right)\left(- 3\right) + \left(- 5\right) \left(-2\right)\right|$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|15 + 9 + 10\right|$

$= 17 . . . \left(1\right)$

Area of $ACD = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|∑ {x}_{1}\left({y}_{2} - {y}_{3}\right)\right|$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|3\left(1 - y\right) + \left(-5\$right)\left($y - 4\right) + $x\left($4 - 1\right)\right|$

$= $\dfrac{1}{2} \left|$3 - 3y - 5y + 20 + 3x\right|$

$= $\dfrac{1}{2}\left|+$3x - 8y + 23\right| . . . \left($2\right)$

From equations~$( 1 )$~and $( 2 )$,

\pm ( +$3x - 8y + 23 ) = 34$

$⇒ 3x - 8y + 23 = $\pm$34$

$⇒ 3x - 8y + 23 = 34$~or $3x - 8y + 23 = - 34$

$⇒ 3x - 8y - 11 = 0$~or $3x - 8y + 57 = 0$

$∴$ The locus of $D$ is \left($3x - 8y - 11\$right)\left($3x - 8y + 57\right) = 0$.

questions.q: If the axes are rotated through an angle $45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$ in the positive direction without changing the origin, then the co-ordinates of the point $(\sqrt{2}, 4)$ in the old system are
questions.solution:
If $\theta$ is the angle of rotation, then the co-ordinates in the new system are $x^{\prime}=x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta$, $y^{\prime}=y \cos \theta-x \sin \theta$
Given that $x^{\prime}=\sqrt{2}, y^{\prime}=4$
Thus, $x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta=\sqrt{2}$
y \cos $\theta-$x \sin $\theta=$4 Also, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4} \Rightarrow x \cos \frac{\pi}{4}+y \sin \frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt{2}$
and $y \cos \frac{\pi}{4}-x \sin \frac{\pi}{4}=4\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow$& x+y=2 \\
$\text { and }$& y-x=4 $\sqrt{2}
\end{array}$On adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $2 y=2+4 \sqrt{2}\Rightarrow \quad y=1+2 \sqrt{2}$
On subtracting (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & 2 x & =2-4 $\sqrt{2}$\\
& x & =1-2 $\sqrt{2}
\end{array} \Rightarrow \quad$x=1-2 $\sqrt{2}$Thus, the co-ordinates of $(\sqrt{2}, 4)$ in the old system $(1-2 \sqrt{2}, 1+2 \sqrt{2})$

questions.solution:
Since $\triangle P Q R$ is isosceles right angled triangle. Hence $\angle P Q R=\angle P R Q=45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$
Let $m_1$ and $m_2$ be the slope of line $P Q$ and line $P R$ respectively. Given line $Q R$ is $2 x+y=3\Rightarrow y=-2 x+3$. Hence slope of $Q R=m=-2$ Since the angle between $P Q$ and $R Q$ is $45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$. Hence $\begin{aligned}$& \tan 45^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}=$\frac{m_1-m}{1+m_1 m}=\frac{m_1+2}{1-2 m_1}$\\ & \Rightarrow m_1+2=1-2 m_1 \Rightarrow 3 m_1=-1 \\ & \Rightarrow m_1=-$\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$Since $P R$ and $P Q$ are perpendicular lines Hence $m_1 m_2=-1$ \Rightarrow m_2=-$\frac{1}{m_1}=$3 \Rightarrow m_2=3 Hence equation of line $P Q$, $\begin{aligned}$& y-1=m_1(x-2)=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)($x-2) \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow 3 y+x+1=0 \end{aligned} Hence equation of line $P R$, $\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } \Rightarrow y-1=m_2(x-2)=3(x-2) \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow 3 x-y-5=0 \end{aligned} $

questions.solution:
We can assume that OP and OR are x–axis and y–axis respectively.

Let OP = a, then area (square OPQR) = a2
Coordinate of M and N are $\left(a, \dfrac{a}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{a}{2}, a\right)$ respectively.
∴ area (∆OMN) = $\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\begin{cases}a & a / 2 \\ a / 2 & a\end{cases}\right] = \dfrac{3{a}^{2}}{8}$
∴ $\dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{\lambda}{6}$
∴ λ = 16
⇒ $\dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{16}{4} = 4$

questions.solution:
Given $L \equiv x-y-4=0 ⇒ \frac{x}{(-4)}+\frac{y}{(4)}=$1 Slope $m_1$ of line ' $L$ ' is $m_1=1$
Since line ' $L$ ' and line $P Q$ is parallel to each other. Hence slope of line ' $L$ ' $=$ Slope of line $P Q$ Hence equation of $P Q$ can be written as $\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow y-1=m_1(x-2)=(1)(x-2) \\ & \Rightarrow y=(x-1) \\ & \because $\text { Distance }$P Q=2 $\sqrt{3}$\\ & \Rightarrow $\sqrt{(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2}=$2 $\sqrt{3}$\\ & \Rightarrow(x-2)^2+(x-2)^2=12 \\ & \Rightarrow(x-2)^2=6 \\ & \Rightarrow(x-2)= $\pm \sqrt{6} \text { or }$x=2+$\sqrt{6} \text { or }$2-$\sqrt{6} \end{aligned}$Here $x=2+\sqrt{6}$ is not valid because point $Q$ lies in third quadrant. Hence $x=2-\sqrt{6}$ Therefore $y=(2-\sqrt{6})-1=1-\sqrt{6}$ \therefore Q(x, y)=Q(2-$\sqrt{6},$1-$\sqrt{6})$Let the slope of line perpendicular to given line ' $L$ ' is $m_2$. Then, m_1 m_2=-1 \Rightarrow m_2=-$\frac{1}{m_1}=-\frac{1}{1}=-$1 Hence equation of line perpendicular to ' $L$ ' and passing through point $Q(2-\sqrt{6}, 1-\sqrt{6})$ will be $\begin{aligned}$& y-(1-$\sqrt{6})=$m_2[x-(2-$\sqrt{6})]=-$1(x-2+$\sqrt{6})$\\ & \Rightarrow y-1+$\sqrt{6}=-$x+2-$\sqrt{6}$\\ & \Rightarrow x+y=3-2 $\sqrt{6} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the lines $x+2 a y+a=0, x+3 b y+b=0$, $x+4 c y+c=0$ are concurrent, then $a, b$ and $c$ are in
questions.solution:
Let these three lines be $L_1, L_2$ and $L_3\begin{aligned}
& L_1=x+2 a y+a=0 \\
& L_2=x+3 b y+b=0 \\
& L_3=x+2 c y+c=0
\end{aligned}$
If $L_1, L_2$ and $L_3$ are concurrent, then
\left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 2 a & a \\
1 & 3 b & b \\
1 & 4 c & c
\end{array}\right|=0$
Applying $R_1 \rightarrow R_1-R_2, R_2 \rightarrow R_2-R_3$,
$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
0 & 2 a-3 b & a-b \\
0 & 3 b-4 c & b-c \\
1 & 4 c & c
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1[(2 a-3 b)(b-c)-(3 b-4 c)(a-b)]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(2 a-3 b)(b-c)=(3 b-4 c)(a-b) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 a b-2 c a-3 b^2+3 b c=3 a b-3 b^2-4 c a+4 b c \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a b+b c=2 c a \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{2}{b}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $a, b$ and $c$ are in Harmonic progression.$

questions.solution: Let line $\mathrm{AB}$ be $\mathrm{x}+3 \mathrm{y}=7$ and point $\mathrm{P}$ be $(3,8)$. Let $\mathrm{Q}$ (h, k) be the image of point $P(3,8)$ in the line $x+3 y=7$. Since line $\mathrm{AB}$ is a mirror. (1) Point $\mathrm{P} \ \text{ and } \mathrm{Q}$ are at equal distance from line $\mathrm{AB}$ i.e. $P R=Q R$ i.e. $R$ is the mid-point of $P Q$. (2) Image is formed perpendicular to mirror i.e. line $P Q$ is perpendicular to line $\mathrm{AB}$. Since $\mathrm{R}$ is the midpoint of $\mathrm{PQ}$. Mid point of $\mathrm{PQ}$ joining $(3,8)$ and $(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$ is  \left(\frac{\mathrm{h}+3}{2}, \frac{\mathrm{h}+8}{2}\right)$ Coordinate of point $\mathrm{R}= $\$left(\frac{\mathrm{h}+3}{2}, \frac{\mathrm{h}+8}{2}\right) Since point $\mathrm{R}$ lies on the line $\mathrm{AB}$. Therefore, $\$left(\frac{3+\mathrm{h}}{2}\right)+$3\$left(\frac{8+\mathrm{k}}{2}\right)=$7$ \Rightarrow \mathrm{h}+3 \mathrm{k}=-13.....(i) Also, $\mathrm{PQ}$ is perpendicular to $\mathrm{AB}$ Therefore, slope of $\mathrm{PQ} \times$ Slope of $\mathrm{AB}=-1\Rightarrow$ Slope of $\mathrm{PQ} \times\$left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)=-$1\Rightarrow$ Slope of $\mathrm{PQ}=3$ Now, $\mathrm{PQ}$ is the line joining $\mathrm{P}(3,8)$ \ \text{ and } $\mathrm{Q}(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$. $\therefore$ Slope of $\$mathrm{PQ}=3=\frac{\mathrm{k}-8}{\mathrm{~h}-3} \Rightarrow$3 \mathrm{~h}-\mathrm{k}=1$.....(ii) Solving eqn. (i) \ \text{ and } (ii), we get $\begin{aligned}$& \mathrm{h}=-1 \& \mathrm{k}=-4 \\ & \therefore \text { Image is } \mathrm{Q}(-1,-4)=(\alpha, \beta) \Rightarrow \alpha=-1, \beta=-4 \\ & \alpha+\beta=-1+(-4)=-5 \end{aligned} $
